content.text:
Recommend one multi-stage `docker/Dockerfile`, four final targets, and one release workflow.

| Target | Entrypoint/default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `binary` | `exposed`; default `server` | Preserve existing general-purpose image behavior |
| `frontend-server` | supervisor launching Rust and nginx | Serve static frontend and API on one public port |
| `migrate` | `exposed migrate`; default `run --source /app/db/migrations` | One-shot migration job |
| `data` | `exposed data`; default `--help` | Existing data CLI, with caller-supplied subcommands |

All inherit a shared Debian runtime containing the same compiled binary. Only `migrate` copies migrations; only `frontend-server` adds nginx, frontend assets, and its launcher. Keep the last/default target equivalent to `binary` so untargeted builds remain compatible.

A separate frontend builder runs the locked Node install and Vite build. nginx serves `dist`, provides SPA fallback, and proxies `/api/` to `http://127.0.0.1:6999/`; the trailing slash removes the prefix. Handle exact `/api` explicitly, and ensure API failures never fall through to `index.html`. Use a nonprivileged public port and writable nginx temporary paths.

For combined process handling, use `tini` plus a small Bash supervisor. Start nginx in foreground and `exposed server` as children; `wait -n` detects either exit. On child exit, stop and reap its sibling and fail the container, including when the child unexpectedly exits zero. On TERM/INT, forward shutdown to both and reap both. This is smaller than adding a general supervisor, and safer than `nginx & exposed server`. Test both child-crash paths and container shutdown explicitly.

Separate Dockerfiles would isolate ownership but duplicate runtime, dependency, and binary-copy rules. Here the variants differ chiefly in entrypoint and payload, so named targets express the differences with fewer places to drift.

Release flow:

1. Build all four targets locally on the runner with shared BuildKit cache.
2. Smoke-test every built image before registry publication: CLI help; migrations against a disposable PostgreSQL instance; offline `data latest` using a mounted empty data directory; combined static root, SPA route, API proxy, and lifecycle behavior.
3. After all pass, allocate the UTC release tag and publish those exact locally tested images. Avoid rebuilding during publication.
4. Record each registry digest in a release manifest and publish one GitHub release after all four uploads succeed.

Preserve `ghcr.io/<repo>:<release>` and existing `image.txt` for the binary image. Add `<release>-frontend-server`, `<release>-migrate`, and `<release>-data`, plus a structured manifest listing all four immutable `repository@sha256:…` references. Avoid publishing a multi-image Docker manifest list to represent variants: manifest lists select platforms, not application modes.

Expand workflow paths and `.dockerignore` allowlists to cover frontend files, all Docker support files, and migrations. A single shared cache writer avoids competing jobs overwriting one cache scope; if builds later become a matrix, give targets separate write scopes.

Caveats: the migrate target requires the CLI migration branch; choose that base before implementation. Local image loading and push must preserve the tested image identity; retaining BuildKit provenance may require OCI artifacts rather than the default Docker image store. Registry publication cannot be atomic across four tags: failed uploads must prevent the GitHub release, and the release manifest becomes the authoritative complete set.
